name: boxd
oneLiner: KVM machines in the EU that boot in milliseconds, snapshot with memory, fork live, and hibernate when idle.
whatItIs: boxd sells persistent Linux virtual machines: each one a KVM guest with its own kernel, root, systemd and a fixed 100 GB copy-on-write disk. They boot in milliseconds, can be copied while running, and park themselves when idle.
The pattern it is built for is: compose one machine by hand (install tools, sign into agents, leave a service running), save it as a snapshot, then stamp out identical machines from it.
It is one product sold three ways: pay-as-you-go credits, a Custom contract with SSO and audit logs, and a self-hosted version you run on your own hardware.
whoFor: Developers and teams who want a normal Linux server that happens to be a VM, with fast copies: dev workspaces, preview environments, coding agents, one machine per customer.
isolation: KVM microVM with its own kernel, network stack and disk, on boxd's open-source Ignition orchestrator. Docker, systemd, kernel modules and breaking the OS are all allowed and stay inside that one machine. Firecracker use is not documented.
sizes: Four sizes named by either dimension: 1 vCPU / 4 GiB, 2 / 8 (the default), 4 / 16, 8 / 32. Disk is fixed at 100 GB and is not a size choice.

billing.model: Prepaid credits, no plan and no per-seat fee.
billing.meter: Per second, settled every 15 minutes, on three meters: vCPU on the machine's size while running, RAM on resident memory while running or in standby, disk on bytes written in every state.
billing.stopped: Disk only. Hibernated and stopped machines pay for written disk; a machine in standby keeps paying for RAM.
billing.planFee: None. Custom and self-hosted are contracts with unpublished prices.
billing.minimum: No minimum charge per machine. There is no free plan: $30 of credit requires a card, and an account without one is capped at two machines.

A.headline: ≈ $25.03 or $34.37 a month
A.shape: 2 vCPU / 8 GiB (the nearest size), 4 GiB resident, 2 GiB written, deleted after each task
notes: If a task fills the shape at 8 GiB resident, the same work costs $34.37.
RAM is billed on what the machine holds, so the 8 GiB size does not force an 8 GiB bill.

B.headline: ≈ $222.50 or $304.26 a month
B.shape: 4 vCPU / 16 GiB (the only 4 vCPU size), 8 GiB or 16 GiB resident, 50 GiB written
notes: 8 GiB is a working set, not a purchase: the 4 vCPU shape comes with 16 GiB and bills what it holds.
Sleeping 8 hours a day instead of running always: about $149.60 at 8 GiB resident.

C.headline: ≈ $14.88 or $19.92 a month
C.shape: 2 vCPU / 8 GiB, 4 GiB or 8 GiB resident, 20 GiB written, 90 running hours in a 720-hour month
notes: A 30-day month is 720 hours, so 630 hours are stopped.
Leaving it in standby instead of stopping is the expensive mistake: about $50.16 at 4 GiB, because RAM keeps billing.
Relying on the 4-hour idle hibernate instead of stopping: about $32.88.

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: Registered 5 February 2026; the first public blog post is 14 August 2026. No founding date is published.

facts.label: Funding
facts.value: €2M pre-seed led by BlueYard Capital, announced 16 September 2026. No later round is published.

source.quote: boxd has raised €2 million in pre-seed funding led by BlueYard Capital, with participation from Antler, OVNI, s20, Script Capital and a group of angels who have built developer infrastructure before.

facts.label: Headcount
facts.value: Not published. The blog counts three authors, which is a floor rather than a headcount.

facts.label: Status and SLA
facts.value: No status page, no published uptime figure and no SLA. Support is a founder-led 25-minute onboarding call.

facts.label: Certification
facts.value: No SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA or PCI claim on the site, the terms or the privacy notice.

facts.label: Data residency
facts.value: Marketed as EU-only with no US cloud dependency, but the privacy notice describes EU and US clusters on a Delaware infrastructure vendor.

source.quote: Latitude.sh LLC (Delaware, United States): bare-metal server infrastructure for our European Union and United States clusters.

well: A build-and-test workload that needs a fork of memory and disk in 100–200 ms.
A team that wants a KVM machine with its own kernel, Docker, systemd and kernel modules.
EU hosting on German bare metal, with an allowlist enforced outside the machine.
badly: Procurement that needs an SLA, a status page or a certification before signing.
A workload whose cost depends on RAM: memory bills on resident use, also in standby.
Anything needing a REST API, a US region today, or a published egress price.

usability.dashboard: Yes, at boxd.sh/app, with Machines, Backups, Domains, Integrations, Organizations and Billing pages plus a desktop viewer. It is secondary: every guide's first instruction is a CLI command, and the sign-in page leads with Download the CLI.
usability.withoutCode: Partly, and less than the marketing suggests. A non-coder can watch and drive a machine someone else set up (desktop, browser, files), and can copy a prompt for an AI agent to do the setup. There is no template gallery and no one-click agent.
usability.signup: GitHub or Google, then a card for the $30 credit and for more than two machines. There is no waitlist in the EU; the US region has one. Every account starts with a 25-minute onboarding call.
usability.docs: Mintlify docs with a full CLI reference, gRPC proto, SDK references and machine-readable bundles. Support is a founder by email. There is no status page.
tripsUp: The first step is a terminal command: install the CLI, log in, create a machine.
Machine sounds like a physical server you rent; it is a VM that sleeps and keeps charging for disk.
The pricing vocabulary is engineer-facing: resident memory, GiB-hour, written disk.
The headline hourly price assumes 2 GiB of an 8 GiB machine is in use.
Whatever you serve is on the open internet at name.boxd.sh, with no auth in front.
Sleep is invisible: a cron job or long build stops when the machine hibernates, and the clock freezes.

caveats.issue: The bill follows resident RAM, not the shape
caveats.detail: A 4 vCPU machine is 16 GiB, but boxd bills the memory it actually holds: $222.50 a month at 8 GiB resident and $304.26 at 16 GiB. boxd's own calculator assumes 2 GiB on an 8 GiB machine, which is a best case rather than a typical one.

caveats.issue: Public URLs are open, and bot protection gates only wake-ups
caveats.detail: There is no authentication in front of name.boxd.sh. Bot protection is on by default, but it only asks a browser check when a request would wake a sleeping machine, and it applies to the main address, never to subdomain proxies or custom domains. A webhook, API client or uptime monitor that hits a sleeping machine gets a 503 check page and the machine does not wake.

caveats.issue: The machine quota is stated as both 50 and 100
caveats.detail: Docs and FAQ say 50 machines per organisation; the pricing page says 100 included, raiseable on request.

evidence.quote: Machines | 50 per organization (your default org included)

caveats.detail: The docs say every machine's domain points at the proxy's shared public IP, and SSH runs on a dedicated port on that shared proxy IP. The FAQ says machines come with a public IPv4. No price for an inbound IPv4 is published. Both statements are current, so the answer is unresolved.

evidence.quote: persistent, forkable Linux VMs with their own kernel, a public IPv4, and an automatic HTTPS domain
Every machine's domain points at the proxy's shared public IP.

caveats.issue: EU-only, except for the US cluster in its own privacy notice
caveats.detail: The FAQ says managed boxd runs on EU hardware with no US cloud dependency. The privacy notice names a Delaware infrastructure vendor and two clusters, and says choosing the US cluster transfers data to the United States. The residency answer depends on which page you read.

evidence.quote: Managed boxd runs on EU hardware with no US cloud dependency, GDPR / DSGVO by default, and no exposure to US subpoenas.
If you choose our United States Cluster… your data may be transferred to and processed in the United States.

caveats.detail: No boxd page mentions a dedicated or static outbound address, and none prices one. battleships.dev lists it as a feature. We could not confirm it, so it is neither offered nor ruled out here.
The 9 October capture showed €0.049/vCPU-hour, €0.015/GiB-hour and 50 machines; the 28 October page shows €0.039, €0.012 and 100 machines. Any cost figure needs a date.
Snapshots, checkpoints, backups and extra disks all exist, and none has a published price. Egress has no price or allowance either.

caveats.issue: No status page and no REST API
caveats.detail: status.boxd.sh does not resolve and boxd.sh/status is a 404. The only wire API is gRPC; there is no HTTP/JSON endpoint for machines.

strengths: A live fork that copies memory and disk in 100–200 ms.
Snapshots that keep memory, so new machines come up already running.
Secrets bound to a host: the machine holds an opaque placeholder, never the key.
EU-only residency on German bare metal, plus a self-hosted option.
Four state tools with distinct jobs: snapshot, checkpoint, backup, fork.
